extracted.intended_audience: communication scholars, crisis communication researchers, public relations practitioners, and crisis managers
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly summary and critical assessment of W. Timothy Coombs' Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT), focused on its framework for classifying crises, selecting response strategies, and protecting organizational reputation. Useful for researchers evaluating the theory and practitioners deciding how (and whether) to apply it in real crisis situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis classification framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The core of the model is a framework that supports the classification of crisis situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the framework to categorize the type of crisis as a first step; classification guides which response strategies are appropriate. Note that later commentary questions whether crisis types deterministically determine perceived responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of appropriate response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework supports identification of possible response strategies tailored to crisis type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose response strategies aligned with the classified crisis type; Coombs' earlier work ('Choosing the right words') provides guidelines for selecting 'appropriate' crisis-response strategies. Timing of responses is also important (see Claeys & Cauberghe, 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaping attribution of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT claims to shape attributions of responsibility in a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses should aim to influence stakeholder perceptions of who is responsible. Be aware that attributions are also influenced by stakeholders' prior knowledge and multiple information sources, making deterministic mappings from crisis type to attribution unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing public perception of the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT aims to change the public's perception of the organization following a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether chosen communication strategies alter stakeholders' views; reputation outcomes are a primary evaluation metric for strategy effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating negative effects on organization
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT seeks to mitigate the negative effects of the crisis on the organization (reputation mitigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact in terms of reputational damage reduction and other organizational consequences; mitigation is a central goal of strategy selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing and experimental validation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory has been 'extensively tested and further developed in numerous experiments' according to the chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate SCCT claims against experimental and meta-analytic evidence (e.g., Ma & Zhan, 2016; Coombs, 2016). Empirical support strengthens confidence in recommended strategies; lack thereof is a criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic versus empirical value
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism points to SCCT's deficits and its status as more heuristic than empirically definitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying SCCT, distinguish between its heuristic usefulness (a guiding framework) and strong empirical generalizations. Treat prescriptive claims cautiously if empirical backing is limited or context-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicability for crisis managers (early decision-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT claims to be application-oriented, but critics argue it may not provide concrete help for crisis managers who must make early decisions with limited information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the theory offers actionable guidance for first-responder communications (what to say, to which stakeholders, and when). The chapter notes that lab-tested pattern types may be of limited direct use in early, real-world decision contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of stakeholders' prior knowledge and multiple information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions and responsibility perceptions are influenced by prior knowledge of the organization and the number of information sources stakeholders use in crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for stakeholder heterogeneity and information environments; do not assume a single attribution outcome based solely on crisis type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate crises by reputational risk (beyond attributed blame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises should be described not only by attributed blame but also differentiated by the content-specific reputational risk they pose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and prioritize crises according to the particular reputational dimensions threatened (e.g., competence, integrity, safety) rather than relying solely on assignment of blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability across industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Coombs draws on experiences from several industries in developing the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether recommended strategies generalize across sectors; industry-specific norms and stakeholder expectations may alter strategy effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of past crises' impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact of past crises on current crisis communications is a factor discussed in SCCT literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate organizational crisis history into strategy selection—prior incidents can change stakeholder expectations and attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social media influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Later revisions of SCCT address the influences of social media on crisis communication theory and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include channel effects, speed, and social-media-specific dynamics (e.g., viral spread, stakeholder-organized blame) when applying SCCT in contemporary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to stakeholder emotions and affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder emotions (affect) play a role in crisis perception and response effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design responses that consider and, where appropriate, address stakeholder emotions; empirical studies examine how affect interacts with attributions and strategy outcomes.
